cards.question: What is a model, in this course?
answers: A simplified rule that predicts an output from inputs
A fast answer to a question that used to be slow
An exact copy of reality
A 3D model of a building
cards.explanation: Our first model predicts heating demand from compactness. It is simplified on purpose; nobody claims it is the building.

cards.question: What is a neuron, in the sense used in this course?
answers: Inputs, one weight each, a bias, one output
A simulation of a biological nerve cell
The building block of every network in this course
A table of measured values
cards.explanation: It is a weighted input plus a bias. The biological name is historical; nothing in it models a real nerve cell.

cards.question: In the line  prediction = w × compactness + b,  what do w and b do?
answers: w sets how steeply the prediction rises with compactness
b lifts or lowers the whole line
w is the heating demand of the house
b is the number of buildings
cards.explanation: w is the slope, also called the weight; b moves the whole line up or down, also called the bias.

cards.question: What are the parameters of a model?
answers: Its adjustable numbers, such as w and b
What the learning loop changes
The table of buildings
The learning rate you choose
cards.explanation: You choose the learning rate; the loop finds the parameters.

cards.question: What is a loss?
answers: One number saying how wrong the model is
What the learning loop tries to make smaller
The number of buildings the model gets wrong
The heat lost through a wall
cards.explanation: Ours is the mean squared error. Smaller means a better line.

cards.question: How do you compute the mean squared error?
answers: Square each miss, then take the average
Add up the misses without squaring
Take the largest miss
cards.explanation: Squaring stops misses above and below from cancelling, and makes one big miss count more than several small ones.

cards.question: What does the gradient tell you?
answers: How much the loss changes per unit you move a parameter
Which way to go: step against its sign
Where the minimum is
How many steps are left
cards.explanation: It is the slope where you stand. Negative means going right lowers the loss; it says nothing about how far the bottom is.

cards.question: What is gradient descent?
answers: Repeatedly stepping against the gradient
What your learning loop does, thousands of times
Solving for the best line in one go
Trying every possible w
cards.explanation: Solving in one go is least squares; gradient descent walks there step by step.

cards.question: What does the learning rate do?
answers: It is multiplied by the gradient to give the step
If it is too large, the loss explodes instead of falling
It is learned by the model
It sets how many buildings are used
cards.explanation: new w = old w − learning rate × gradient. On our buildings, a learning rate of 0.03 already tips over.

cards.question: What is the method of least squares?
answers: Choosing the line whose squared misses add up to the least
Published by Legendre and Gauss around 1805
A method that needs a neural network
A way to measure heating demand
cards.explanation: It finds the best straight line directly. Your loop arrives at the same line by walking.

cards.question: Your building has a residual of +5 kWh/m²a. What does that mean?
answers: The table value is 5 above what the line predicts
The line guessed too low for this building
The line guessed too high
The building needs 5 kWh/m²a
cards.explanation: Residual = table value (later: measured value) minus prediction. Positive: the line was too low.
